method: Notes are read as scientific pitch notation, with C4 at MIDI 60 and A4 at the 440 Hz reference, so a note's MIDI number is (octave + 1) x 12 plus its pitch class and accidental. Frequencies follow 12-tone equal temperament: f = 440 x 2^((midi - 69) / 12). The range is the difference between the two MIDI numbers, split into whole octaves and remaining semitones, and its frequency ratio is 2^(semitones / 12). Six common classical and choral reference ranges are compared: a range is reported as containing the singer's notes when both reference endpoints lie outside the sung range, as overlapping when the two spans share at least one pitch, and otherwise as outside, and the narrowest containing range is named. Head voice, falsetto, passaggio, tessitura and any Fach classification are not modelled, and reference ranges differ between traditions, so the comparison is descriptive rather than a diagnosis. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Scientific pitch notation: C4 is MIDI note 60 and A4 is the 440 Hz reference
Common classical and choral voice ranges, approximately: bass E2-E4, baritone G2-G4, tenor C3-A4, alto F3-F5, mezzo-soprano A3-A5, soprano C4-C6
